What if the Sun... suddenly disappeared?
For about eight minutes, nothing would happen. Sunlight already on its way would keep arriving.
Even Earth's orbit wouldn't change yet, because gravity travels at the speed of light too.
Then, eight minutes and twenty seconds later, the sky goes black.
A second later, the Moon goes dark. But Jupiter keeps shining for over an hour, lit by old sunlight.
With nothing to orbit, Earth flies off in a straight line, at thirty kilometers per second, taking the Moon with it.
Plants stop making food, and most of them die within weeks.
Within a week, the average temperature drops below freezing. Within a year, it could reach around minus seventy degrees.
The oceans freeze over. But the ice acts like a blanket, keeping the water underneath liquid for a very long time.
Deep down, life around hydrothermal vents doesn't need sunlight at all. It lives on heat and chemicals from inside the Earth.
People could survive too, deep underground, powered by geothermal heat and nuclear energy.
Eventually, it gets so cold that the air itself freezes, and falls as snow.
Earth becomes a rogue planet, drifting alone through the galaxy. There may be billions of them out there.
Luckily, the Sun isn't going anywhere. It should keep shining for about five billion more years.
